name_zh: 大吉岭麝香葡萄风味红茶
processing: Darjeeling black tea, normally second flush, from young leaves bitten by jassids and thrips. The plant's response raises terpene levels, which helps form the flavour; the leaf is then processed as usual.
harvest_season: Mainly the second flush, the summer picking of Darjeeling; muscatel is the prized note of that season.
appearance_dry: Twisted brown leaf with some silvery or golden tips, darker than first flush.
appearance_wet: Mostly coppery brown leaf with some green.
taste_profile: Sweet muscat-grape fruit, sometimes described as raisin with a hay-like finish and a musky spiciness, over a medium body.

brewing.notes: Hotter water than first flush brings out the fruit. Taste it plain, since milk hides the very note you paid for.

vintage_note: Sold as second flush by estate and harvest year, with 'muscatel' appearing as a descriptor on the label rather than as a controlled grade. It does not appear in every lot, partly because it depends on insect feeding. Current-year tea is the usual choice, and it keeps better than first flush.
description:
Muscatel is a flavour before it is a product: a sweet, grapey, slightly musky note found in some Darjeeling teas, especially second flush. Shops use it as a name, and tea drinkers chase it, but no separate tea or grade stands behind the word.

The unusual part is the cause. Jassids and thrips feed on young leaves, and the plant answers with more terpenes as a repellent. Those compounds are part of the note in the finished cup, so a little insect damage is what makes the tea.

Good examples taste of muscat grape or raisin, with a touch of hay and spice. Brew it with hotter water than first flush and try it plain. Sweetness sits in the aroma, so sip it while it is still warm.

Since anyone can write muscatel on a packet, buy second flush from a named estate and year, and rely on tasting notes only from sellers you trust. A sample before a big purchase is well worth it, as the note varies from lot to lot.
history: The note is tied to Darjeeling's second flush and is not reported from other flushes or from tea of other places in the same form. When drinkers first began using the word is poorly documented. The explanation through insect feeding and terpenes is modern, and it turned a taster's word into something with a known mechanism, at least in part.
